item.title: Lasawa elected Methodist Church President Elect for 2027
item.description: Reverend Dr Jolami Lasawa has been elected President Elect of the Methodist Church in Fiji for 2027, following leadership elections at the Church’s Annual Conference today. His election was one of the major outcomes of Day Three of the Methodist Church in Fiji Annual Conference 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Reverend Dr Jolami Lasawa has been elected President Elect of the Methodist Church in Fiji for 2027, following leadership elections at the Church’s Annual Conference today.

His election was one of the major outcomes of Day Three of the Methodist Church in Fiji Annual Conference 2026.

Rev Dr Lasawa will assume the presidency in 2027 and provide spiritual and pastoral leadership to one of Fiji’s largest Christian denominations as it continues its mission and ministry in Fiji and abroad.

The Conference also elected current Methodist Church President Reverend Dr Semisi Turagavou as General Secretary Elect for 2027.

Rev Dr Turagavou’s election will see him transition from the presidency to the senior administrative position next year.

Meanwhile, elections were also conducted for the position of Assistant General Secretary, currently held by Reverend Dr Anil Reuben.

The result is expected to be announced tomorrow.

Rev Dr Reuben’s current five-year term as Assistant General Secretary concludes in April 2027.

Apart from the leadership elections, Conference members continued deliberations on a range of issues affecting the Church and its institutions.

Matters relating to the Davuilevu Theological College, Deaconess Order and Women’s Fellowship were among those discussed.

Representatives of the institutions and departments were given opportunities to respond to questions and provide clarification on issues raised by Conference members.

The discussions form part of the Church’s efforts to strengthen theological education, ministry, fellowship and its wider institutional operations.

The Methodist Church in Fiji Annual Conference continues this week, with further deliberations and leadership announcements expected.

Attention will now turn to the remaining elections and discussions as the Church prepares for a significant leadership transition in 2027.

item.title: US visa suspension overturned
item.description: FIJIAN nationals planning to permanently migrate to the United States have received a significant boost after a US federal court struck down a policy that suspended immigrant visa issuance to citizens of Fiji and 74 other countries. The United States District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled on Friday that the nationality-based policy was contrary to law and exceeded the statutory
item.content:encoded:
FIJIAN nationals planning to permanently migrate to the United States have received a significant boost after a US federal court struck down a policy that suspended immigrant visa issuance to citizens of Fiji and 74 other countries.

The United States District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled on Friday that the nationality-based policy was contrary to law and exceeded the statutory authority of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The court ordered the policy vacated under the Administrative Procedure Act.

Fiji was among the 75 countries targeted under the policy introduced by the US Department of State in January.

The suspension, which took effect on January 21, was based on concerns that immigrants from the designated countries were at higher risk of using welfare or becoming a “public charge”.

Under the directive, consular officers were required to refuse immigrant visas to nationals of the listed countries even where an individual assessment found an applicant was otherwise eligible.

The court found this approach unlawful, noting US immigration law prohibits discrimination in the issuance of immigrant visas based on nationality.

The ruling is particularly significant for Fijians pursuing family-based or employment-based permanent migration to the United States.

The court ordered that the policy categorically suspending immigrant visas for nationals of the 75 countries be set aside. It also ordered that visa refusals based solely on the policy be vacated and returned for further consideration.

However, the decision does not automatically mean every affected Fijian applicant will receive a visa.

The court made clear that its order does not overturn refusals where applicants were found ineligible on other grounds under US immigration law.

The judgment effectively removes nationality alone as the barrier imposed by the January policy, restoring the opportunity for affected applicants to have immigrant visa applications considered under the normal statutory requirements.

item.title: ‘Motherhood penalty’
item.description: FIJIAN mothers are facing a “motherhood penalty” at work, with limited breastfeeding support and potential income losses when they take time off to care for sick children, says perinatal support group Mama Talanoa founder Mercedes Swann. Speaking during a dialogue on postpartum depression, Mrs Swann said policy changes were needed to better support women during pregnancy and after childbirth.
item.content:encoded:
FIJIAN mothers are facing a “motherhood penalty” at work, with limited breastfeeding support and potential income losses when they take time off to care for sick children, says perinatal support group Mama Talanoa founder Mercedes Swann.

Speaking during a dialogue on postpartum depression, Mrs Swann said policy changes were needed to better support women during pregnancy and after childbirth.

She called for extended maternity leave and workplace arrangements that allow mothers to breastfeed, express and safely store breast milk after returning to work.

She said mothers could also face financial pressure when they stayed home to care for sick children or during floods, cyclones and school closures.

“There really is this motherhood penalty going on where mothers are penalized at work because they are a mom for simply being a mom.”

Mrs Swann said cultural attitudes also made it difficult for women to speak openly about mental health.

“In our Fijian culture it is very much taboo to talk about mental health.

“We just have this culture of just get through it and you’ll be fine.”

She said families often focused on the newborn while overlooking the mother’s wellbeing.

“A baby was born, yes, but a mother was also born.”

She called for safe spaces and stronger support from families, communities and churches.

item.title: Calls for stronger support
item.description: AS the Fiji Police Force intensifies its fight against drugs, police mothers are facing another battle — balancing demanding frontline duties with motherhood and the risk of postpartum depression. Speaking at a postpartum depression dialogue, police Psychologist Unit officer Litia Raiwalui said women officers were often expected to remain strong because of their frontline roles.
item.content:encoded:
AS the Fiji Police Force intensifies its fight against drugs, police mothers are facing another battle — balancing demanding frontline duties with motherhood and the risk of postpartum depression.

Speaking at a postpartum depression dialogue, police Psychologist Unit officer Litia Raiwalui said women officers were often expected to remain strong because of their frontline roles.

“Drugs, that’s the main focus right now,” she said.

Ms Raiwalui said mental health struggles had long been treated as issues to be kept private.

“We don’t talk about this, we are told to be strong.”

She said police mothers could work 12-hour shifts and be deployed over weekends, adding pressure as they balanced their professional and family responsibilities.

Ms Raiwalui said postpartum depression required greater recognition within the force and officers needed better access to psychoeducation to recognise its warning signs.

“We are frontliners, so we have to be okay.”

However, she said being a frontline officer should not mean suppressing mental health struggles or challenges associated with motherhood.

Ms Raiwalui said stronger support systems were needed to help police mothers continue serving while receiving the support they needed.

She said creating an environment where officers could speak openly about their struggles was essential to ensuring their wellbeing was not sacrificed in the line of duty.

item.title: HIV crisis hits young iTaukei mothers
item.description: NINE in 10 pregnant women diagnosed with HIV in Fiji are iTaukei, raising concern over the growing impact of the virus on young women and their families. Ministry of Health and Medical Services principal medical officer for Sexual and Reproductive Health and HIV Unit Harm Reduction lead Dr Sailosi Soqo revealed the figures while speaking at the 43rd Fiji Head Teachers Association annual conference
item.content:encoded:
NINE in 10 pregnant women diagnosed with HIV in Fiji are iTaukei, raising concern over the growing impact of the virus on young women and their families.

Ministry of Health and Medical Services principal medical officer for Sexual and Reproductive Health and HIV Unit Harm Reduction lead Dr Sailosi Soqo revealed the figures while speaking at the 43rd Fiji Head Teachers Association annual conference in Nadi.

Dr Soqo said the women were often young mothers whose children were part of the school system.

“These are young women, sisters, mothers of children who are in your classroom,” he said.

He said only 10 per cent of the partners of women diagnosed with HIV came forward for testing, meaning the majority remained untested.

Dr Soqo also raised concern about people seeking treatment at an advanced stage of the disease.

“Almost a third that come to us have advanced HIV.”

He said 90 per cent of people who died from HIV in 2025 had been diagnosed in 2016, adding that some patients died within the same year they presented for treatment.

item.title: inDepth I Welfare cover axed
item.description: THE Government has ended a controversial social welfare insurance scheme after paying about $60 million in taxpayers’ money over eight years, with only $33.8 million reaching beneficiaries through direct claims. Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran told Parliament last week that the decision to discontinue the scheme was fiscally responsible and necessary, arguing that to
item.content:encoded:
THE Government has ended a controversial social welfare insurance scheme after paying about $60 million in taxpayers’ money over eight years, with only $33.8 million reaching beneficiaries through direct claims.

Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran told Parliament last week that the decision to discontinue the scheme was fiscally responsible and necessary, arguing that too much public money was being absorbed by insurance costs rather than reaching vulnerable Fijians.

The scheme, introduced in 2018, was initially designed to increase insurance penetration among civil servants and social welfare recipients. Civil servants were later removed because of the high cost of maintaining their coverage.

Under the scheme, Government paid quarterly premiums for eligible welfare recipients, covering areas including term life, funeral expenses, personal accidents and fire.

But Ms Kiran said the numbers showed a significant mismatch between what Government paid and what beneficiaries received.

“Over the past eight years, the Government has diligently paid approximately $60 million in hard-earned taxpayers’ funds to FijiCare Insurance as premiums,” she said.

“However, a deeper dive into the metrics reveals a stark and troubling imbalance.”

Of the $60 million paid in premiums, only $33.8 million was paid out to citizens as direct claims.

In 2023-2024, Government paid $7.1 million in premiums but received claims payouts totalling only $3.8 million.

The following year, premiums increased to $7.2 million while payouts remained at $3.8 million.

In 2025-2026, premiums rose again to $7.7 million, but claims fell to $3 million.

Ms Kiran said the figures demonstrated that the insurance model was failing to deliver value for public money.

“On average, a mere 56 per cent of the total funds paid out by the Government ended up in the hands of the beneficiaries.

“The remaining 44 per cent did not serve our poor. Instead, it was absorbed by administrative friction, overheads and private corporate margins.”

Ms Kiran said Government had been spending roughly $7 million annually to cover about 100,000 welfare recipients, yet only about 5000 claims were processed each year.

“We are paying massive premium blocks for a system where 95 per cent of the covered population see no tangible touchpoint or benefit in any given year.”

She argued that the scheme was particularly inefficient because most recipients did not directly benefit from the insurance during any given year.

Ms Kiran said the data also showed that the primary beneficiaries were often family members rather than elderly welfare recipients themselves.

The scheme provided one-off assistance for life and funeral costs, with payments ranging from $1500 for those under 60 to $500 for seniors aged between 60 and 69.

Fire and personal accident cover provided up to $3000.

However, Ms Kiran pointed to the extremely low number of personal accident claims as evidence of underutilisation.

“Personal accidents under this scheme are extremely rare.

“To highlight this, the entire 2022-2023 financial year, there were only four paid-out accident claims across the nation, costing a total of $10,500.”

Government promises safety-net alternatives

Ms Kiran rejected concerns that ending the insurance scheme would leave welfare recipients without protection.

“I want to assure this House that removing this insurance scheme will have minimal to no impact on the existing social welfare recipients.”

She said Government would continue providing direct assistance through six major social welfare programs.

For the 2026-2027 financial year, the Government has allocated $184 million across the programs.

This includes $46.46 million for the Family Assistance Scheme, more than $18 million for the Child Protection Allowance, more than $82 million for the Social Pension Scheme, over $420,000 for food allowance for rural pregnant mothers, more than $18 million for allowances for persons with disabilities and over $14 million for the Transport Assistance Scheme.

Ms Kiran said the Government believed direct assistance provided a more effective way of supporting vulnerable people than paying large insurance premiums.

item.title: Khan moves to halt asset forfeiture proceedings
item.description: INMATE Imran Khan has filed an urgent High Court application seeking to stay State forfeiture proceedings and preserve assets subject to an active appeal. Khan, currently serving a prison sentence, alongside second appellant Deborah Kim, filed an affidavit on August 21 requesting an order to halt further forfeiture actions by the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) pending their Court of Appeal
item.content:encoded:
INMATE Imran Khan has filed an urgent High Court application seeking to stay State forfeiture proceedings and preserve assets subject to an active appeal.

Khan, currently serving a prison sentence, alongside second appellant Deborah Kim, filed an affidavit on August 21 requesting an order to halt further forfeiture actions by the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) pending their Court of Appeal case.

The application stems from a February 20, 2026, judgment by Justice Senileba Waqainabete-Levaci. The court issued an unexplained wealth declaration and permanent restraint orders over $404,840.34 in a Bred Bank account under Reliable Computers, a Valelevu residential property, and four vehicles.

According to the application, Khan states that while his lawyer only learned of the DPP’s new forfeiture application through media reports, finalising forfeiture before their appeal is heard would render their legal challenge meaningless.

The appellants argue the original ruling erred by relying on speculative opinion evidence without cross-examination and failing to conduct adequate financial analysis.

Khan assured the court they are not seeking the release of the assets, offering to maintain current restraint orders to preserve status quo until the appeal concludes.

item.title: Avoidable backlash
item.description: THE confusion and backlash now erupting across Fiji’s key tourist source markets as a result of the 5 per cent Tourism Services Tax (TST) was avoidable and was flagged to the Government in detail months before the controversial tax was gazetted. The FHTA had continuously raised concerns since the announcement of the levy, and had also proposed simpler and less disruptive ways to support Fiji Airwa
item.content:encoded:
THE confusion and backlash now erupting across Fiji’s key tourist source markets as a result of the 5 per cent Tourism Services Tax (TST) was avoidable and was flagged to the Government in detail months before the controversial tax was gazetted.

The FHTA had continuously raised concerns since the announcement of the levy, and had also proposed simpler and less disruptive ways to support Fiji Airways directly rather than a blunt tax bolted onto the wider tourism supply chain.

According to the FHTA, the Australian Travel Industry Association had called the tax’s retrospective application to existing bookings “an absolute no-go”, and accused Fiji of a fundamental misunderstanding of how the travel booking ecosystem, worked.

“We tried to make this work from day one and we were ignored at every turn,” FHTA chief executive officer Fantasha Lockington said in a statement.

“We asked that pre-booked and paid holidays be exempted, the same treatment given under the old Service Turnover Tax. We asked for clarity on the sunset clause. Both requests were left out of the final Gazette, without explanation.”

She said they had also asked for a minimum of four weeks between the release of the Fiji Revenue and Customs Service’s Standard Interpretation Guidelines and the tax’s implementation date, given how much narrower the TST’s scope was compared with the STT it replaced.

“The guidelines were not finalised until yesterday, 10 days before the tax takes effect on September 1.

“We handed government a clear, specific warning of exactly how complicated this was going to be to administer.

“That warning was not heard, or it was heard and dismissed.

“Either way, the result is the mess our travel partners are now scrambling to clean up, with days rather than weeks to do it.”

Ms Lockington said agents managing multi-resort itineraries had described a process with no consistent collection method, forcing them to re-invoice wholesalers, re-invoice clients, and reconcile bookings that were settled months ago.

She said New Zealand agents had raised the same alarm at the Fiji roadshow events in Christchurch last week.

“Tourism Fiji and this industry have spent years and a great deal of money building Fiji’s name as a credible, well-run destination in markets with no shortage of alternatives.

“That reputation is being damaged this week, not because of the tax itself, but because Government would not listen when we told them exactly how to avoid this outcome.”

She said with the guidelines only finalised last week, travel agents, wholesalers and tour operators now had a little over a week to overhaul booking systems, invoicing processes and client communications before the tax takes effect.

“Our industry is not against Fiji investing in its own aviation sector.

“What we needed was consultation, time and clarity, and we asked for all three, repeatedly, well before this became a crisis.”
